deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a reading excerpt, in English, from John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Chapter 21 ('Of Power'). It carries a German heading, 'Über Freiheit und Determinismus' (On freedom and determinism), and a few German or Latin glosses by the writer. The structure follows Locke's own marginal section headings, each quoted with „…":

- §5 is cited first; '§4 cc' is struck out.
- §31 'Uneasiness determines the will' is paired with §37: only present uneasiness can operate, since 'what is absent' cannot 'operate, where it is not'.
- §8 'Liberty, what': freedom is the power to think or not think, and to move or not move, according to the preference of one's own mind.
- §9 'Supposes the Understanding and Will'.
- §15: in a parenthesis, volition is distinguished from 'preferring'. One may prefer flying to walking without willing it. Volition is 'an Act of the Mind, knowingly exerting that Dominion it takes it self to have over any Part of the Man'.
- §§10–13 'Belongs not to Volition', §§14–20 'belongs not to the Will', §21 'But to the Agent or Man': the proper question is not whether the will is free but whether a man is free.
- §§22–24 'In respect of willing a Man is not free': once an action in his power is proposed to his thoughts as presently to be done, he cannot avoid willing.
- §25 'The will determined by something without it': to ask whether a man is free to will which of motion or rest he pleases is absurd. The writer adds his own gloss '(series infinita)', marking the infinite regress of willing to will.
- §29 'What determines the will': the mind; more precisely, the motive to change is always some uneasiness. The '§37 (s. o.)' means 'siehe oben', i.e. see above.
- §39: uneasiness accompanies the other passions (aversion, fear, anger, envy, shame) and is always joined with desire.

The neighbouring pages are excerpts from Herbart: the previous page cites Werke VII, 175, and the next page cites the Encyklopädie §§238 ff. This Locke excerpt therefore belongs to Riemann's philosophical and psychological reading around Herbart's treatment of freedom and will. There are no derivations to reconstruct.

results.what: Excerpt of Locke's analysis of liberty and will (Essay II.21, §§5–39), with a marginal note that the question 'free to will what one wills' leads to an infinite regress
results.modern_name: Lockean compatibilist account of freedom / regress argument against 'freedom of the will'

deep.surprise_reason: Philosophical reading notes copying Locke nearly verbatim, consistent with Riemann's known Herbart-related studies in the Naturphilosophie papers. No mathematical or original content.
transcription_corrections: Heading reading 'Über Freiheit und Determinismus' appears correct.
Left margin at top shows section marks stacked (struck '§.4' and '§.31'). '§.31' matches Locke's marginal heading 'Uneasiness determines the will'.
'yet who[?] can say he ever wills it' — the hand looks like 'yet ho'. Locke's text reads 'yet who can say he ever wills it?', so 'who' is correct.
'(series infinita)' is the writer's own Latin gloss, not part of Locke's text. '(s. o.)' after §37 = 'siehe oben'.
'Liberty, what' is written above the §8 line as an inserted marginal heading.
